evidence.title: Risk assessment and quality management in AIO based on CT-linac for nasopharyngeal carcinoma: An improved FMEA and FTA approach
evidence.effect: Automated pre-planning ROI check reduced RPN from 186.2 to 35.3.
evidence.quote: This significantly reduced its RPN from 186.2 to 35.3, substantially decreasing the risk associated with this FM.

evidence.title: Auditor models to suppress poor artificial intelligence predictions can improve human-artificial intelligence collaborative performance
evidence.effect: When ML outperformed humans, suppression outperformed human alone (P < 8.2 × 10-6) and did not degrade fairness; when humans outperformed ML, humans were fairer than suppression (P < 8.2 × 10-4) or no different.
evidence.quote: When the ML outperforms humans, suppression outperforms the human alone (P < 8.2 × 10-6) and at least does not degrade fairness.
evidence.sample_unit: patient records (VUMC n=58,817; MIMIC-IV-ED n=363,145) with simulated clinician acceptance

evidence.title: A Real-World Evaluation of Failure Detection for Liver CT Segmentation
evidence.outcome: Ability of output-based failure detectors to flag implausible or failed segmentations
evidence.effect: Pairwise Surface DSC detected segmentation failures with sensitivity 1.00 and balanced accuracy 0.94 internal, 0.88 external.
evidence.quote: These results show that automated failure detection for liver CT segmentation is clinically feasible and that Pairwise Surface DSC is a promising candidate for deployment.
evidence.country: Multinational (internal data plus external data from ~70 sites in 7 countries)

evidence.title: Automatic contour quality assurance using deep-learning based contours
evidence.outcome: ability of post-processing comparison metrics to flag dosimetric errors
evidence.effect: including dose metrics increased ROC-AUC and PR-AUC for H&N small structures for D_error,mean, and for small, medium, and GYN structures for D_error,max
evidence.quote: In many instances, utilizing dose with geometric comparisons can improve the ability of a verification model to flag potential errors from a primary auto-contouring model.

evidence.title: Selective segmentation with rejection option: a machine reasoning approach and evaluation metrics in CT kidney segmentation
evidence.outcome: False positives and anatomically invalid kidney segmentations with reasoning-based rejection versus LCCA
evidence.effect: Reasoning-based approaches (FMR, AR, LCCAPS) reduced false positives and anatomically invalid outputs more than LCCA while preserving acceptance of valid candidates; results persisted under noise. No numbers in abstract.
evidence.quote: Reasoning-based approaches (FMR, AR, and LCCAPS) reduced false positives and anatomically invalid outputs more effectively than LCCA, while preserving acceptance of valid segmentation candidates.
evidence.sample_unit: CT kidney segmentation cases (KiTS23, five validation folds)

evidence.title: Dual site external validation of artificial intelligence-enabled treatment monitoring for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in England
evidence.effect: 18/37 (48.6%) NEC R9 errors not made in real-world care had non-anatomical IRF/SRF segmentations.
evidence.quote: For the 37 errors that R9 led to in the NEC dataset, which were not made in real-world care, 18 (48.6%) involved segmentations of IRF or SRF that were immediately apparent as non-anatomical on clinical review (Fig. 3 ).

commentary.bottom_line: Five offline or benchmark studies suggest that postprocessing checks can flag failed or implausible segmentation and dosimetry outputs, but none measured whether blocking those outputs changed clinician decisions or patient outcomes. Support for the practice comes from one consensus guideline and from technical performance data in imaging and radiotherapy.

perspectives.view: All five tests of the practice were offline or benchmark evaluations. Samples ranged from 5 to 500 cases, and outcomes were limited to detection accuracy or risk scores. The results point in the same direction, but indirectness, small samples, and the absence of clinical endpoints lower certainty to very low.

In an English retinal clinic replay, 18 of 37 (48.6%) AI errors not made in real-world care involved non-anatomical fluid segmentations, which shows the failure mode exists. A failure mode analysis reported that an automated check lowered the risk priority number from 186.2 to 35.3. A multinational benchmark detected segmentation failures with sensitivity 1.00.

No study placed a check inside a live workflow, so alert burden and clinician response remain unmeasured. The French cohort reported recall 0.75 and precision 0.88, which implies that about one in four failures would pass and some valid outputs would be flagged. Balanced accuracy fell from 0.94 internally to 0.88 externally, which suggests performance may drop at new sites.

No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two tests did not report a country. Only the hazard study described its population, which was older adults. No study examined whether detection thresholds hold across different scanners or across patient groups at under-resourced sites.

commentary.research_gap: No study has embedded output checks in a deployed clinical system. Such studies should measure how often implausible outputs are blocked, how often valid outputs are wrongly rejected, and whether clinician decisions and patient outcomes change. Tests outside imaging and radiotherapy, and tests in safety-net settings, are also needed.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the five tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these checks perform equally well for those patients or at sites with older equipment and different case mixes.
